```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
library(truncnorm)
library(rstan)
rstan_options(auto_write = TRUE)
```

The last two chapters drew from a **fixed** proposal $g$: an envelope for rejection sampling, an importance distribution for reweighting. Both work well when $g$ can be made to resemble the target $f$ over its whole support, but in more than a handful of dimensions no fixed $g$ does — the target occupies an ever-thinner sliver of the space $g$ covers, exactly the curse of dimensionality met already for quadrature grids. **Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)** answers this differently: instead of one global proposal, build a **random process** $\theta^{(0)}, \theta^{(1)}, \theta^{(2)}, \ldots$ that moves *locally* — each step depends only on where the chain currently is — and is engineered so that, after enough steps, $\theta^{(t)}$ is (approximately) distributed as the target $f$. The price is that consecutive draws are dependent and the guarantee is only asymptotic; the payoff is that the same local-move idea scales to any dimension.

This chapter develops the Markov chain theory that makes this work, then builds three increasingly automatic ways to construct such a chain — Gibbs sampling, Metropolis–Hastings, and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo — and ends with Stan, which automates the last of these for essentially arbitrary models. Each method is presented first as theory, followed by one or more examples, each named after the problem it solves. A final section applies Stan to a practical problem, a sparse logistic regression with as many predictors as cases, and compares it with `glm` and the LASSO.

## Markov Chains

### Definition and the convergence question

A sequence $\theta^{(0)}, \theta^{(1)}, \theta^{(2)}, \ldots$ is a **Markov chain** if the future depends on the past only through the present,
$$
P\big(\theta^{(i)} \mid \theta^{(0)}, \ldots, \theta^{(i-1)}\big) = T\big(\theta^{(i)} \mid \theta^{(i-1)}\big),
$$
where $T$, the **transition distribution**, does not depend on $i$. A chain is completely specified by a starting value (or distribution) and $T$; simulating it just means repeatedly drawing $\theta^{(i)} \sim T(\cdot \mid \theta^{(i-1)})$.

A distribution $\pi$ is the **equilibrium** (or limiting) distribution of the chain if, for every starting value $\theta^{(0)}$,
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty} P\big(\theta^{(n)} = \theta \mid \theta^{(0)}\big) = \pi(\theta):
$$
after many steps the chain forgets where it started. The usual Markov-chain question is *given $T$, find $\pi$*. MCMC reverses it: given a target $\pi$ known only up to a constant, can we *design* a $T$ such that, no matter where the chain starts, $\theta^{(i)}$ converges in distribution to $\pi$ as $i \to \infty$? If so, running the chain for a long time and averaging $a(\theta^{(i)})$ over the later iterations estimates $E_\pi[a(\theta)]$ — this is what "MCMC" means in practice.

### Invariance, detailed balance, and convergence

$\pi$ is an **invariant** (or stationary) distribution of transition $T$ if
$$
\int \pi(\theta)\, T(\theta \to \theta') \, d\theta = \pi(\theta') \qquad \text{for all } \theta'.
$$
In words: if $\theta \sim \pi$ and one step of the chain is applied, the result is again distributed as $\pi$ — $\pi$ is a fixed point of $T$. Invariance alone does not guarantee the chain *converges* to $\pi$ from an arbitrary start (a chain that never moves leaves every distribution invariant), so two more conditions are needed: **aperiodicity** (the chain does not cycle deterministically through a fixed sequence of states) and **irreducibility** (every state can eventually be reached from every other). Under all three, $\theta^{(i)} \to \pi$ in distribution from any starting point, and ergodic averages converge, $\frac1n\sum_i a(\theta^{(i)}) \to E_\pi[a(\theta)]$.

Invariance is a *global* condition (it involves integrating over all $\theta$) and is awkward to check directly for a proposed $T$. The standard shortcut is a *local*, pairwise condition. $T$ satisfies **detailed balance** with respect to $\pi$ if
$$
\pi(\theta)\, T(\theta \to \theta') = \pi(\theta')\, T(\theta' \to \theta) \qquad \text{for all } \theta, \theta',
$$
i.e. the flow of probability from $\theta$ to $\theta'$ under $\pi$ exactly balances the reverse flow (the transition $T$ itself need not be symmetric — only the $\pi$-weighted flow is). Detailed balance implies invariance: integrating both sides over $\theta$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\int \pi(\theta)\, T(\theta \to \theta') \, d\theta
&= \int \pi(\theta')\, T(\theta' \to \theta) \, d\theta \\
&= \pi(\theta') \underbrace{\int T(\theta' \to \theta)\, d\theta}_{=\,1} = \pi(\theta').
\end{aligned}
$$
Every construction in this chapter — Gibbs, Metropolis–Hastings, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo — is a recipe for building a $T$ that satisfies detailed balance (or, for Gibbs, invariance directly) with respect to a *given* target $\pi$, so that simulating the chain long enough and discarding an initial **burn-in** period produces (dependent) draws from $\pi$.

### Example 1: Two Random Walks on a Cycle

The machinery above can be run in the direction opposite to MCMC: take a transition $T$ and *find* its equilibrium by solving the detailed-balance equations. Consider two chains on the eleven states $\{0, 1, \ldots, 10\}$ arranged on a circle, with indices taken mod 11, so that $10$ and $0$ are neighbours and $5$ sits in the middle. At each step a chain moves to one of its two neighbours or stays put, and the two chains differ only in the probabilities:

- the **cyclic walk** moves forward (clockwise) with probability $0.45$, backward with probability $0.45$, and stays with probability $0.1$;
- the **walk toward 5** moves to the neighbour *closer to 5* with probability $0.4$, to any other neighbour with probability $0.2$, and stays with the remaining probability.

Writing $d(i) = |i - 5|$ for the distance from $i$ to $5$ (which is also the distance around the circle), the second chain has, for a neighbour $j = i \pm 1$,
$$
T_5(i \to j) = \begin{cases} 0.4, & d(j) < d(i) \quad (\text{toward } 5), \\ 0.2, & \text{otherwise}, \end{cases}
\qquad T_5(i \to i) = 1 - T_5(i \to i+1) - T_5(i \to i-1),
$$
so the probability of staying is $0.4$ at every state except $5$, where both moves lead away from $5$ and it is $0.6$. The neighbours $10$ and $0$ are both at distance $5$, so a move between them is "other" in both directions and has probability $0.2$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-two-walks-diagram
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-cap: "Shows the transition structure of two random walks on eleven states arranged on a circle.
#|   Left: the cyclic walk, which moves to either neighbour with probability 0.45. Right: the walk
#|   toward 5, which moves toward state 5 (thick blue arrows) with probability 0.4 and in any other
#|   direction (thin red arrows) with probability 0.2."
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5), cex = 1.1)
ang <- -pi / 2 - 2 * pi * ((0:10) - 5) / 11; rr <- 0.13; dl <- 0.11   # clockwise, 5 at the bottom
draw_cycle <- function(main, col_fwd, col_bwd, lwd_fwd, lwd_bwd, node_bg = rep("white", 11)) {
    plot(NA, xlim = c(-1.45, 1.45), ylim = c(-1.35, 1.35), asp = 1, axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", main = main)
    for (i in 0:10) {
        a1 <- ang[i + 1]; a2 <- ang[(i + 1) %% 11 + 1]
        arrows(1.07 * cos(a1 - dl), 1.07 * sin(a1 - dl), 1.07 * cos(a2 + dl), 1.07 * sin(a2 + dl),
               length = 0.07, col = col_fwd[i + 1], lwd = lwd_fwd[i + 1])        # i -> i + 1 (clockwise)
        arrows(0.93 * cos(a2 + dl), 0.93 * sin(a2 + dl), 0.93 * cos(a1 - dl), 0.93 * sin(a1 - dl),
               length = 0.07, col = col_bwd[i + 1], lwd = lwd_bwd[i + 1])        # i + 1 -> i
    }
    symbols(cos(ang), sin(ang), circles = rep(rr, 11), inches = FALSE, add = TRUE, bg = node_bg, lwd = 2)
    text(cos(ang), sin(ang), 0:10)
}
draw_cycle("cyclic walk", rep("gray40", 11), rep("gray40", 11), rep(1.8, 11), rep(1.8, 11))
text(0, 0.1, "each move 0.45", col = "gray30"); text(0, -0.1, "stay 0.1", col = "gray30")
## clockwise i -> i + 1 is toward 5 for i = 0, ..., 4; i + 1 -> i is toward 5 for i = 5, ..., 9;
## the pair (10, 0) is at equal distance from 5, so 0.2 both ways
toward_fwd <- (0:10) <= 4; toward_bwd <- (0:10) >= 5 & (0:10) <= 9
draw_cycle("walk toward 5",
           ifelse(toward_fwd, "steelblue", "firebrick"), ifelse(toward_bwd, "steelblue", "firebrick"),
           ifelse(toward_fwd, 3, 1.5), ifelse(toward_bwd, 3, 1.5), node_bg = ifelse(0:10 == 5, "gold", "white"))
text(0, 0.2, "toward 5: 0.4", col = "steelblue"); text(0, 0, "other: 0.2", col = "firebrick")
text(0, -0.2, "stay: the rest", col = "gray30")
```

**Detailed balance only involves neighbours.** In both chains $T(i \to j) = 0$ unless $j$ is a neighbour of $i$, so for non-neighbours both sides of the detailed-balance equation are $0$, and for $i = j$ the equation is trivial. Only the eleven neighbouring pairs $(i, i+1)$ need to be checked, and the stay probabilities never enter.

**The cyclic walk.** For every pair,
$$
\pi(i)\, T(i \to i+1) = \pi(i+1)\, T(i+1 \to i)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
0.45\, \pi(i) = 0.45\, \pi(i+1)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\pi(i+1) = \pi(i),
$$
so going around the circle $\pi(0) = \pi(1) = \cdots = \pi(10)$ and, normalizing, $\pi_{\text{cyc}}(i) = 1/11$. By the theorem above this $\pi$ is invariant; the chain is irreducible (every state is reached by moving around the circle) and aperiodic (it can stay put), so the uniform distribution is its equilibrium. Every state has the same local picture, so the equilibrium treats them all alike.

**The walk toward 5.** In every neighbouring pair except $\{10, 0\}$, one state $j$ is one step closer to $5$ than the other state $i$, and detailed balance reads
$$
\pi(i)\, \underbrace{T(i \to j)}_{0.4\ (\text{toward})} = \pi(j)\, \underbrace{T(j \to i)}_{0.2\ (\text{away})}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\pi(j) = 2\, \pi(i),
$$
while the pair $\{10, 0\}$, both at distance $5$, gives $0.2\,\pi(10) = 0.2\,\pi(0)$. Each step closer to $5$ doubles $\pi$, so $\pi(i) \propto 2^{-|i-5|}$, and normalizing with $\sum_i 2^{5 - |i-5|} = 32 + 2(16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1) = 94$,
$$
\pi_5(i) = \frac{2^{\,5 - |i-5|}}{94}, \qquad i = 0, 1, \ldots, 10.
$$
The equations are consistent around the circle ($\pi$ doubles five times from $0$ up to $5$, halves five times down to $10$, and $\pi(10) = \pi(0)$), and the chain is irreducible and aperiodic, so this is its equilibrium: symmetric, with a peak of $32/94 \approx 0.34$ at $5$, falling by half for each step away.

**Empirical check.** Each chain is simulated by a one-line step function that, given the current state and a uniform draw $u$, returns the next state:

```{r}
#| label: sim-walks
cyc_step <- function(s, u)
    ifelse(u < 0.45, (s + 1) %% 11, ifelse(u < 0.9, (s - 1) %% 11, s))
toward5_step <- function(s, u) {
    fwd <- (s + 1) %% 11; bwd <- (s - 1) %% 11
    p_fwd <- ifelse(abs(fwd - 5) < abs(s - 5), 0.4, 0.2)     # toward 5: 0.4, other: 0.2
    p_bwd <- ifelse(abs(bwd - 5) < abs(s - 5), 0.4, 0.2)
    ifelse(u < p_fwd, fwd, ifelse(u < p_fwd + p_bwd, bwd, s))
}
sim_chain <- function(step, ini, iters) {
    mc <- integer(iters + 1); mc[1] <- ini
    for (i in 2:(iters + 1)) mc[i] <- step(mc[i - 1], runif(1))
    mc
}
set.seed(1)
cyc <- sim_chain(cyc_step, 2, 20000)
tw5 <- sim_chain(toward5_step, 2, 20000)
pi_cyc <- rep(1 / 11, 11); pi_5 <- 2^(5 - abs(0:10 - 5)) / 94       # from detailed balance
freq <- function(mc) as.vector(table(factor(mc[-(1:200)], levels = 0:10))) / length(mc[-(1:200)])
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-two-walks
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Confirms the equilibrium distributions found from detailed balance by simulating the two random walks.
#|   One chain of each kind, started at state 2 and run for 20,000 steps. Top: the first 300 steps. Bottom:
#|   long-run frequencies of the states after discarding 200 steps (bars), against the equilibrium from
#|   detailed balance (points): uniform for the cyclic walk, and 2^(5 - |i - 5|)/94 for the walk toward 5."
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(cyc[1:300], type = "s", col = "steelblue", xlab = "step", ylab = "state", ylim = c(0, 10),
     main = "cyclic walk: first 300 steps", yaxt = "n"); axis(2, at = 0:10, las = 1)
plot(tw5[1:300], type = "s", col = "firebrick", xlab = "step", ylab = "state", ylim = c(0, 10),
     main = "walk toward 5: first 300 steps", yaxt = "n"); axis(2, at = 0:10, las = 1)
bp <- barplot(freq(cyc), names.arg = 0:10, col = "lightsteelblue", ylim = c(0, 0.4),
              xlab = "state", ylab = "frequency", main = "cyclic walk: uniform, 1/11")
points(bp, pi_cyc, pch = 19, col = "steelblue4", cex = 1.3)
bp <- barplot(freq(tw5), names.arg = 0:10, col = "mistyrose", ylim = c(0, 0.5),
              xlab = "state", ylab = "frequency", main = "walk toward 5")
points(bp, pi_5, pch = 19, col = "firebrick4", cex = 1.3)
legend("topleft", bty = "n", pch = c(15, 19), col = c("mistyrose", "firebrick4"), pt.cex = c(2, 1.3),
       legend = c("observed frequency", "equilibrium from detailed balance"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-two-walks
#| tbl-cap: "Compares the long-run state frequencies of the two simulated random walks with their equilibrium distributions from detailed balance.
#|   Frequencies over 20,000 steps after discarding the first 200."
tab <- rbind("cyclic walk, frequency" = freq(cyc), "cyclic walk, equilibrium" = pi_cyc,
             "walk toward 5, frequency" = freq(tw5), "walk toward 5, equilibrium" = pi_5)
colnames(tab) <- 0:10
knitr::kable(tab, digits = 3)
```

The observed frequencies agree with the equilibria found from detailed balance up to Monte Carlo error. The two chains differ only in their transition probabilities, yet one spreads its time evenly over the circle and the other concentrates around state $5$: the equilibrium is determined entirely by $T$, and the pairwise detailed-balance equations are the easiest way to read it off. MCMC turns this around: it starts from the target $\pi$ and chooses a $T$ whose detailed-balance equations $\pi$ satisfies.

## Gibbs Sampling

### The idea and why it works

Suppose $\theta = (\theta_1, \theta_2)$ and both full conditionals $\pi(\theta_1 \mid \theta_2)$ and $\pi(\theta_2 \mid \theta_1)$ can be sampled directly, even though the joint $\pi(\theta_1, \theta_2)$ has no closed form or cannot be sampled directly. The **Gibbs sampler** alternates
$$
\theta_1^{(t)} \sim \pi\big(\theta_1 \mid \theta_2^{(t-1)}\big), \qquad
\theta_2^{(t)} \sim \pi\big(\theta_2 \mid \theta_1^{(t)}\big).
$$
Each half-step leaves $\pi$ invariant: if $(\theta_1, \theta_2) \sim \pi$, then $\theta_2 \sim \pi(\theta_2)$ (its marginal), and replacing $\theta_1$ by a fresh draw from $\pi(\theta_1 \mid \theta_2)$ produces a pair with joint density $\pi(\theta_2)\,\pi(\theta_1 \mid \theta_2) = \pi(\theta_1, \theta_2)$ — exactly $\pi$ again. Cycling through both coordinates therefore also leaves $\pi$ invariant, and as long as the full conditionals are everywhere positive the chain is irreducible and aperiodic. No proposal, no acceptance step, no tuning: Gibbs sampling only needs full conditionals that can be sampled.

### Data augmentation

Gibbs sampling extends immediately to models with **latent variables**. If the
target $\pi(\theta)$ is awkward but can be written as the marginal of a joint
density $\pi(\theta, z)$ over $\theta$ and some extra unknowns $z$,
$$
\pi(\theta) = \int \pi(\theta, z)\, dz,
$$
then a Gibbs sampler on $(\theta, z)$ that alternates $z \sim \pi(z \mid \theta)$
and $\theta \sim \pi(\theta \mid z)$ has $\pi(\theta, z)$ as its invariant
distribution, so its $\theta$-coordinates are draws from $\pi(\theta)$: the
$z$'s are simply discarded. This **data augmentation** pays off when the
conditionals given $z$ are standard even though $\pi(\theta)$ itself is not.
The $z$ may be real missing data (Example 3, where exact values are hidden
by censoring) or a purely mathematical device (Example 4, where a latent
variance per observation turns a Cauchy likelihood into a normal one).

### Example 2: Normal Data with Unknown Mean and Variance

#### The full conditionals

The running example for this half of the book is $x_1, \ldots, x_n \mid \mu, \sigma^2 \overset{iid}{\sim} N(\mu, \sigma^2)$, with independent priors $\mu \sim N(\mu_0, \sigma_0^2)$ and $\sigma^2 \sim \mathrm{IG}(a_0, \lambda_0)$ (inverse-gamma: $1/\sigma^2 \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(a_0, \lambda_0)$, so $a_0$ is a shape and $\lambda_0$ a rate/scale). The joint posterior is
$$
\begin{aligned}
P(\mu, \sigma^2 \mid x) \ \propto\ {} & e^{-(\mu-\mu_0)^2 / (2\sigma_0^2)} \cdot (\sigma^2)^{-(a_0+1)} e^{-\lambda_0/\sigma^2} \\
& \times (\sigma^2)^{-n/2} \exp\Big\{-\sum_{i=1}^n \tfrac{(x_i-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big\},
\end{aligned}
$$
two-dimensional with no closed-form normalizing constant, but each conditional is standard.

The model is easiest to read as a graph (@fig-dag-normal). Squares are fixed
hyperparameters, open circles are unknown random quantities, shaded circles
are observed data, and each arrow points from a quantity to one whose
distribution depends on it. The box (a *plate*) stands for $n$ copies of what
it contains, one for each observation. The full conditional of a node depends
only on its parents, its children and its children's other parents, which is
why the conditional of $\mu$ needs only its prior constants, the data, and
$\sigma^2$ (the other parent of the data), and likewise for $\sigma^2$.

```{r}
#| label: model-dag-fn
### draw a directed acyclic graph of a Bayesian model:
### squares = fixed hyperparameters, open circles = unknown random quantities,
### shaded circles = observed data (type "observed_square" draws observed data as a
### shaded square; type "dots" is a bare label, e.g. for an omitted stretch of a chain); arrows point from parent to child, and a
### rounded box (plate) holds the quantities repeated over i = 1, ..., n
draw_dag <- function(nodes, edges, plates = list(), main = "", r = 0.33,
                     xlim = range(nodes$x) + c(-0.8, 0.8), ylim = range(nodes$y) + c(-0.8, 0.8)) {
    plot.new(); plot.window(xlim = xlim, ylim = ylim, asp = 1)
    title(main, cex.main = 1)
    for (p in plates) {
        rect(p$x[1], p$y[1], p$x[2], p$y[2], border = "gray45", lwd = 1.5)
        text(p$x[2] - 0.08, p$y[1] + 0.08, p$label, adj = c(1, 0), cex = 0.85, col = "gray30")
    }
    for (k in seq_len(nrow(edges))) {
        a <- nodes[nodes$id == edges$from[k], ]; b <- nodes[nodes$id == edges$to[k], ]
        d <- c(b$x - a$x, b$y - a$y); u <- d / sqrt(sum(d^2))
        arrows(a$x + r * u[1], a$y + r * u[2], b$x - (r + 0.03) * u[1], b$y - (r + 0.03) * u[2],
               length = 0.08, lwd = 1.4, col = if (is.null(edges$col)) "gray20" else edges$col[k])
    }
    th <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 100)
    for (k in seq_len(nrow(nodes))) {
        nd <- nodes[k, ]
        if (nd$type == "dots") {
            # placeholder for the omitted middle of a chain: label only
        } else if (nd$type %in% c("fixed", "observed_square")) {
            rect(nd$x - r * 0.85, nd$y - r * 0.85, nd$x + r * 0.85, nd$y + r * 0.85,
                 col = if (nd$type == "observed_square") "gray80" else "white",
                 border = "gray20", lwd = 1.5)
        } else {
            polygon(nd$x + r * cos(th), nd$y + r * sin(th), border = "gray20", lwd = 1.5,
                    col = if (nd$type == "observed") "gray80" else "white")
        }
        text(nd$x, nd$y, parse(text = nd$label), cex = 1.05)
    }
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-dag-normal
#| fig-width: 4.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Shows the structure of the normal model with unknown mean and variance as a directed graph.
#|   Squares: fixed hyperparameters; open circles: unknown parameters; shaded circle:
#|   observed data. The plate repeats x_i for i = 1, ..., n."
par(mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5))
nodes_norm <- data.frame(
    id    = c("m0", "s0", "a0", "l0", "mu", "s2", "x"),
    label = c("mu[0]", "sigma[0]^2", "a[0]", "lambda[0]", "mu", "sigma^2", "x[i]"),
    x = c(-1.6, -0.6, 0.6, 1.6, -1.1, 1.1, 0), y = c(2, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1, -0.2),
    type = c(rep("fixed", 4), "latent", "latent", "observed"))
edges_norm <- data.frame(from = c("m0", "s0", "a0", "l0", "mu", "s2"),
                         to   = c("mu", "mu", "s2", "s2", "x", "x"))
draw_dag(nodes_norm, edges_norm,
         plates = list(list(x = c(-0.8, 0.8), y = c(-0.9, 0.5), label = "i = 1, ..., n")))
```

**Conditional of $\mu$.** Collect the factors that involve $\mu$ and expand $\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2 = n\mu^2 - 2n\mu\bar x + \sum_i x_i^2$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
P(\mu \mid \sigma^2, x) \ \propto\ \exp\Big\{-\tfrac12\Big[ & \big(\tfrac{1}{\sigma_0^2} + \tfrac{n}{\sigma^2}\big)\mu^2 \\
& - 2\big(\tfrac{\mu_0}{\sigma_0^2} + \tfrac{n\bar x}{\sigma^2}\big)\mu\Big]\Big\},
\end{aligned}
$$
which is the kernel of $N(m, v)$ with $1/v = 1/\sigma_0^2 + n/\sigma^2$ and $m/v = \mu_0/\sigma_0^2 + n\bar x/\sigma^2$ — a precision-weighted average of the prior mean and the sample mean, with $n/\sigma^2$ the weight the data contribute. As $n \to \infty$, $m \to \bar x$ and $v \approx \sigma^2/n$: the prior is overwhelmed.

**Conditional of $\sigma^2$.** Collect the factors involving $\sigma^2$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
P(\sigma^2 \mid \mu, x) & \ \propto\ (\sigma^2)^{-(a_0+1)} e^{-\lambda_0/\sigma^2} \cdot (\sigma^2)^{-n/2} e^{-\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)} \\
& \ =\ (\sigma^2)^{-\left(\frac n2 + a_0 + 1\right)} \exp\Big\{-\tfrac{\lambda_0 + \frac12\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2}{\sigma^2}\Big\},
\end{aligned}
$$
again an inverse-gamma kernel, $\sigma^2 \mid \mu, x \sim \mathrm{IG}\big(\tfrac n2 + a_0,\ \tfrac12\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2 + \lambda_0\big)$: the prior contributes $a_0$ "pseudo-observations" worth of shape and $\lambda_0$ worth of sum-of-squares, and the data add $n$ and $\sum_i(x_i-\mu)^2$ to each.

#### Implementation

We use the weak prior $\mu_0 = 0$, $\sigma_0^2 = 100$, $a_0 = \lambda_0 = 1$, stored once as `mu0`, `s02`, `a0` and `lam0` and reused by every sampler of this model in the chapter. Each line of the loop is one of the two full conditionals above; an inverse-gamma draw is the reciprocal of a gamma draw with the same shape and rate.

```{r}
#| label: gibbs-normal
mu0 <- 0; s02 <- 100; a0 <- 1; lam0 <- 1                       # prior
gibbs_norm <- function(iters, x, mu_init = 0, s2_init = 1) {
    n <- length(x)
    out <- matrix(NA_real_, iters, 2, dimnames = list(NULL, c("mu", "s2")))
    mu <- mu_init; s2 <- s2_init
    for (t in seq_len(iters)) {
        v  <- 1 / (1 / s02 + n / s2)                            # mu | sigma^2, x ~ N(m, v)
        mu <- rnorm(1, v * (mu0 / s02 + sum(x) / s2), sqrt(v))
        s2 <- 1 / rgamma(1, shape = n / 2 + a0, rate = sum((x - mu)^2) / 2 + lam0)   # IG
        out[t, ] <- c(mu, s2)
    }
    out
}
```

A preallocated matrix filled by a plain `for` loop replaces the original `replicate()`-with-`<<-` pattern: it does the same work with one direct assignment per iteration instead of a closure mutating variables in its enclosing scope, and it makes the recurrence — each row built from the previous one — visually explicit.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gibbs-demo
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6.5
#| fig-cap: "Demonstrates the Gibbs sampler on a normal model with unknown mean and standard deviation, using trace plots to check convergence and densities to summarize the posterior.
#|   Gibbs sampler on 50 simulated N(10, 2^2) observations: trace plots
#|   and posterior densities for mu and sigma, with the weak prior."
set.seed(2)
x <- rnorm(50, 10, 2)
draws_gibbs <- gibbs_norm(10000, x)
burn <- 1:200
mu_g  <- draws_gibbs[-burn, "mu"]
sd_g  <- sqrt(draws_gibbs[-burn, "s2"])

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(mu_g, type = "l", col = "steelblue", xlab = "iteration", ylab = expression(mu), main = "trace of mu")
plot(density(mu_g), col = "steelblue", lwd = 2, main = "posterior density of mu", xlab = expression(mu))
plot(sd_g, type = "l", col = "firebrick", xlab = "iteration", ylab = expression(sigma), main = "trace of sigma")
plot(density(sd_g), col = "firebrick", lwd = 2, main = "posterior density of sigma", xlab = expression(sigma))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-gibbs-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Summarizes the posterior distribution obtained from the Gibbs sampler.
#|   Posterior summaries from the Gibbs sampler (after discarding a 200-iteration burn-in)."
gibbs_summary <- data.frame(
    parameter = c("mu", "sigma"),
    mean = c(mean(mu_g), mean(sd_g)),
    sd   = c(sd(mu_g), sd(sd_g)),
    q025 = c(quantile(mu_g, 0.025), quantile(sd_g, 0.025)),
    q975 = c(quantile(mu_g, 0.975), quantile(sd_g, 0.975))
)
knitr::kable(gibbs_summary, digits = 3,
             col.names = c("parameter", "mean", "sd", "2.5%", "97.5%"),
             align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

Because each update changes one coordinate while holding the other fixed, the path of a Gibbs sampler on the joint posterior is a staircase of horizontal and vertical moves (@fig-gibbs-path). From a poor start the chain reaches the bulk of the posterior within a few iterations.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gibbs-path
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-cap: "Shows how the Gibbs sampler moves on the joint posterior of the normal model, one coordinate at a time.
#|   Left: the first 30 moves from the poor start (8, 8) (triangle) over the contours of the exact posterior;
#|   each move is horizontal (a mu update) or vertical (a sigma^2 update). Right: trace plots of the first
#|   100 iterations of the main run."
set.seed(21)
d2 <- gibbs_norm(30, x, mu_init = 8, s2_init = 8)
lpost <- function(mu, s2) sum(dnorm(x, mu, sqrt(s2), log = TRUE)) + dnorm(mu, mu0, sqrt(s02), log = TRUE) -
    (a0 + 1) * log(s2) - lam0 / s2
mg <- seq(7.5, 11.5, length.out = 100); sg <- seq(1.5, 9, length.out = 100)
Z <- outer(mg, sg, Vectorize(lpost)); Z <- exp(Z - max(Z))
layout(matrix(c(1, 1, 2, 3), 2)); par(mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
contour(mg, sg, Z, nlevels = 8, drawlabels = FALSE, xlab = expression(mu), ylab = expression(sigma^2),
        main = "Gibbs path: first 30 moves from (8, 8)")
pp <- rbind(c(8, 8)); for (t in 1:30) pp <- rbind(pp, c(d2[t, 1], pp[nrow(pp), 2]), d2[t, ])   # horizontal then vertical
lines(pp, col = "firebrick", lwd = 1.5); points(d2, pch = 19, col = "firebrick", cex = 0.7)
points(8, 8, pch = 17, cex = 1.5)
plot(draws_gibbs[1:100, "mu"], type = "l", xlab = "t", ylab = expression(mu), main = "trace of mu")
plot(draws_gibbs[1:100, "s2"], type = "l", xlab = "t", ylab = expression(sigma^2), main = "trace of sigma^2")
```

### Example 3: Interval-Censored Normal Data

**The problem.** The quantities of interest are
$x_1, \ldots, x_n \mid \mu, \sigma^2 \overset{iid}{\sim} N(\mu, \sigma^2)$, with the
priors of Example 2, but not every $x_i$ is seen exactly. For each unit we
observe a pair $(I_i, \delta_i)$:

- $\delta_i = 1$ means $x_i$ is **not censored**: it is observed exactly, and
  $I_i = \{x_i\}$.
- $\delta_i = 0$ means $x_i$ is **censored**: we only learn an interval
  $I_i = [a_i, b_i)$ that contains it. The interval may be bounded (a value
  recorded only to the nearest decade, or between two inspection times) or
  open-ended, $b_i = \infty$ (a value known only to exceed a detection or
  follow-up limit, which is right censoring).

The observed data are the $(I_i, \delta_i)$, and the censored $x_i$ are
unknown. The indicators $\delta_i$ are independent of the $x_i$ and of
$(\mu, \sigma^2)$, so they carry no information about the parameters, and the
likelihood is
$$
\begin{aligned}
L(\mu, \sigma^2) = {} & \prod_{i:\,\delta_i = 1} \frac{1}{\sigma}\,\varphi\Big(\frac{x_i - \mu}{\sigma}\Big) \\
& \times \prod_{i:\,\delta_i = 0} \Big[\Phi\Big(\frac{b_i - \mu}{\sigma}\Big) - \Phi\Big(\frac{a_i - \mu}{\sigma}\Big)\Big],
\end{aligned}
$$
where $\varphi$ and $\Phi$ are the standard normal density and CDF. The
products of $\Phi$ differences make the posterior non-standard: neither
conditional of $\mu$ or $\sigma^2$ is a normal or inverse-gamma distribution.

**Data augmentation.** Treat the unobserved $x_i$ as extra unknowns. Given all
$x_i$, the data are complete and the conditionals of $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$ are
exactly those of Example 2. Given $(\mu, \sigma^2)$ and the observed
$(I_i, \delta_i)$, a censored $x_i$ has density proportional to the
$N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ density times the indicator that $x_i \in I_i$:
$$
x_i \mid \mu, \sigma^2, I_i, \delta_i = 0 \ \sim\ N(\mu, \sigma^2) \text{ truncated to } [a_i, b_i),
$$
while an uncensored $x_i$ is fixed at its observed value. One Gibbs iteration is
$$
\begin{aligned}
x_i^{(t)} & \sim P\big(x_i \mid \mu^{(t-1)}, \sigma^{2(t-1)}, I_i, \delta_i\big) \quad (\text{censored } i), \\
\mu^{(t)} & \sim P\big(\mu \mid x^{(t)}, \sigma^{2(t-1)}\big), \qquad
\sigma^{2(t)} \sim P\big(\sigma^2 \mid x^{(t)}, \mu^{(t)}\big).
\end{aligned}
$$
Integrating the latent $x_i$ out of the augmented model gives back exactly the
likelihood above, since $\int_{a_i}^{b_i} \sigma^{-1}\varphi((x - \mu)/\sigma)\,dx$ is
the bracketed $\Phi$ difference.

In the graph of the model (@fig-dag-censored), $x_i$ is an unknown circle
below the parameters, and the observed interval $I_i$ and indicator $\delta_i$
are shaded squares. $I_i$ contains $x_i$ (and equals it when $\delta_i = 1$), so
$x_i$ is its parent. The indicator $\delta_i$ is independent of $x_i$ and of the
parameters (whether a unit is observed exactly does not depend on its value),
so it has no arrows: it carries no information about $(\mu, \sigma^2)$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-dag-censored
#| fig-width: 4.5
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-cap: "Shows the structure of the interval-censored normal model as a directed graph, with the exact values as latent variables.
#|   The exact value x_i (open circle) is unknown. The observed data (shaded squares) are the
#|   interval I_i that contains x_i and the indicator delta_i, which is 1 when x_i is observed
#|   exactly (I_i is the single point x_i) and 0 when it is censored. delta_i is independent
#|   of x_i and the parameters, so it has no arrows."
par(mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5))
nodes_cens <- rbind(nodes_norm[1:6, ], data.frame(
    id = c("x", "d", "I"), label = c("x[i]", "delta[i]", "I[i]"),
    x = c(0, 1.3, 0), y = c(-0.2, -1.4, -1.4),
    type = c("latent", "observed_square", "observed_square")))
edges_cens <- rbind(edges_norm, data.frame(from = "x", to = "I"))
draw_dag(nodes_cens, edges_cens,
         plates = list(list(x = c(-0.8, 2.0), y = c(-2.1, 0.5), label = "i = 1, ..., n")))
```

The sampler below stores each interval as its endpoints `a`, `b`, with
`a = b = x` for an uncensored unit. The censored $x_i$ are drawn from their
truncated normals with `truncnorm::rtruncnorm`, which also handles $b_i = \infty$:

```{r}
#| label: gibbs-censored
gibbs_norm_censored <- function(iters, a, b, delta) {      # prior constants mu0, s02, a0, lam0 of Example 2
    n <- length(a); cens <- delta == 0
    x <- ifelse(cens, pmin(a + 1, b), a)     # start: exact values, or a point in the interval
    mu <- mean(x); s2 <- var(x)
    out <- matrix(NA_real_, iters, 2)
    for (t in seq_len(iters)) {
        ### censored units: x_i | mu, sigma^2 ~ N(mu, sigma^2) truncated to [a_i, b_i)
        x[cens] <- rtruncnorm(sum(cens), a = a[cens], b = b[cens], mean = mu, sd = sqrt(s2))
        ### complete-data conditionals of Example 2
        v  <- 1 / (1 / s02 + n / s2)
        mu <- rnorm(1, v * (mu0 / s02 + sum(x) / s2), sqrt(v))
        s2 <- 1 / rgamma(1, shape = n / 2 + a0, rate = sum((x - mu)^2) / 2 + lam0)
        out[t, ] <- c(mu, s2)
    }
    list(mu = out[, 1], sd = sqrt(out[, 2]))
}
```

To test it, simulate $n = 200$ values from $N(100, 40^2)$. Each is observed
exactly with probability $0.3$. Otherwise it is censored: values above $150$
are only known to be at least $150$ (right censoring, $I_i = [150, \infty)$),
and the rest are only known to the decade, $I_i = [10k, 10k + 10)$.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-gibbs-censored
#| tbl-cap: "Shows that Gibbs sampling extends to interval-censored data by treating the exact values as latent variables, and that the parameters are still recovered.
#|   n = 200 values from N(100, 40^2): 30% observed exactly, the rest censored to a decade or, above 150, right-censored at 150. The naive estimates treat each censored value as its interval's lower end."
set.seed(3)
n_c <- 200
x_true <- rnorm(n_c, 100, 40)
delta  <- rbinom(n_c, 1, 0.3)
a_obs  <- ifelse(delta == 1, x_true, ifelse(x_true >= 150, 150, floor(x_true / 10) * 10))
b_obs  <- ifelse(delta == 1, x_true, ifelse(x_true >= 150, Inf, a_obs + 10))
fit_cens <- gibbs_norm_censored(5000, a_obs, b_obs, delta)
burn2 <- 1:200
knitr::kable(data.frame(
    quantity = c("exact / interval / right-censored", "mu", "sigma"),
    truth = c(sprintf("%d / %d / %d", sum(delta == 1), sum(delta == 0 & is.finite(b_obs)),
                      sum(is.infinite(b_obs))), "100", "40"),
    naive = c("", sprintf("%.2f", mean(a_obs)), sprintf("%.2f", sd(a_obs))),
    posterior = c("", sprintf("%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)", mean(fit_cens$mu[-burn2]),
                              quantile(fit_cens$mu[-burn2], 0.025), quantile(fit_cens$mu[-burn2], 0.975)),
                  sprintf("%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)", mean(fit_cens$sd[-burn2]),
                          quantile(fit_cens$sd[-burn2], 0.025), quantile(fit_cens$sd[-burn2], 0.975)))
), col.names = c("", "truth", "naive", "posterior mean (95% interval)"), align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"))
```

Censoring removes a great deal of information: most units only say which
decade $x_i$ fell in, and the largest values are only known to exceed $150$.
Treating each censored value as the lower end of its interval biases both
estimates downward, and the naive estimates come with no honest measure of
their uncertainty. The augmented
Gibbs sampler still recovers $\mu$ and $\sigma$, because it imputes each
censored $x_i$ from its conditional distribution given the current parameters
and so propagates the uncertainty about where in $I_i$ it lies.

### Example 4: Cauchy Data with Unknown Location and Scale {#sec-gibbs-cauchy}

**The problem.** Observations $y_1, \ldots, y_n$ are modelled as
$\text{Cauchy}(\mu, \sigma)$, a heavy-tailed model that is robust to outliers:
$$
p(y_i \mid \mu, \sigma) = \frac{1}{\pi\sigma\,\big(1 + r_i^2\big)}, \qquad r_i = \frac{y_i - \mu}{\sigma}.
$$
The priors are $\mu \sim N(\mu_0, \tau^2)$ and $\sigma^2 \sim \mathrm{IG}(a_0, b_0)$,
with density $p(\sigma^2) \propto (\sigma^2)^{-(a_0+1)}e^{-b_0/\sigma^2}$. The
posterior of $(\mu, \sigma^2)$ is proportional to
$e^{-(\mu-\mu_0)^2/(2\tau^2)}\,(\sigma^2)^{-(a_0+1)}e^{-b_0/\sigma^2}\prod_i \sigma^{-1}(1 + r_i^2)^{-1}$.
Neither conditional is a standard distribution, because of the factors
$(1 + r_i^2)^{-1}$. Data augmentation fixes this.

#### Step 1: the Cauchy as a scale mixture of normals

Introduce a latent variance $v_i$ for each observation, with
$$
\begin{aligned}
& y_i \mid \mu, \sigma^2, v_i \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2 v_i), \qquad v_i \sim \mathrm{IG}\big(\tfrac12, \tfrac12\big), \\
& p(v_i) = \frac{(1/2)^{1/2}}{\Gamma(1/2)}\, v_i^{-3/2} e^{-1/(2v_i)} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\, v_i^{-3/2} e^{-1/(2v_i)}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Integrating out $v_i$ gives back the Cauchy density:
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \int_0^\infty p(y_i \mid \mu, \sigma^2, v_i)\, p(v_i)\, dv_i \\
&\quad = \int_0^\infty \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2 v_i}}\, e^{-r_i^2/(2v_i)} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\, v_i^{-3/2} e^{-1/(2v_i)}\, dv_i \\
&\quad = \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma} \int_0^\infty v_i^{-2} \exp\Big\{-\frac{1 + r_i^2}{2v_i}\Big\}\, dv_i \\
&\quad = \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma}\cdot\frac{2}{1 + r_i^2} = \frac{1}{\pi\sigma(1 + r_i^2)},
\end{aligned}
$$
using $\int_0^\infty v^{-2}e^{-c/v}\,dv = 1/c$ (substitute $u = 1/v$). So the
augmented model has exactly the original posterior as its $(\mu, \sigma^2)$
marginal, and a Gibbs sampler on $(v, \mu, \sigma^2)$ samples the Cauchy
posterior once the $v_i$ are ignored.

@fig-dag-cauchy shows this augmented model. Compared with @fig-dag-normal, each
observation has its own latent variance $v_i$, a child of the fixed constants
$\tfrac12, \tfrac12$ of its $\mathrm{IG}$ prior and a parent of $y_i$. Since
$v_i$ has only one child, its full conditional involves only $y_i$, $\mu$ and
$\sigma^2$, as Step 3 below confirms.

```{r}
#| label: fig-dag-cauchy
#| fig-width: 4.8
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-cap: "Shows the structure of the augmented Cauchy model as a directed graph.
#|   Each observation y_i has its own latent variance v_i with a fixed IG(1/2, 1/2) prior;
#|   integrating v_i out gives the Cauchy model for y_i."
par(mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5))
nodes_cauchy <- data.frame(
    id    = c("m0", "t2", "a0", "b0", "mu", "s2", "half", "v", "y"),
    label = c("mu[0]", "tau^2", "a[0]", "b[0]", "mu", "sigma^2", "frac(1, 2)", "v[i]", "y[i]"),
    x = c(-1.6, -0.6, 0.6, 1.6, -1.1, 1.1, -2.4, -1.3, 0),
    y = c(2, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1, -0.2, -0.2, -1.2),
    type = c(rep("fixed", 4), "latent", "latent", "fixed", "latent", "observed"))
edges_cauchy <- data.frame(from = c("m0", "t2", "a0", "b0", "half", "mu", "s2", "v"),
                           to   = c("mu", "mu", "s2", "s2", "v", "y", "y", "y"))
draw_dag(nodes_cauchy, edges_cauchy,
         plates = list(list(x = c(-1.9, 0.6), y = c(-1.9, 0.4), label = "i = 1, ..., n")))
```

#### Step 2: the augmented joint posterior

Multiplying priors, the latent-variable densities and the normal likelihood,
$$
\begin{aligned}
p(\mu, \sigma^2, v \mid y) \propto {} & e^{-\frac{(\mu-\mu_0)^2}{2\tau^2}}
\,(\sigma^2)^{-(a_0+1)} e^{-b_0/\sigma^2} \\
& \times \prod_{i=1}^n \Big[ (\sigma^2 v_i)^{-1/2} \exp\Big\{-\frac{(y_i-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2 v_i}\Big\}
\cdot v_i^{-3/2} e^{-1/(2v_i)} \Big].
\end{aligned}
$$
Each full conditional is read off by keeping only the factors that contain the
parameter being updated and recognizing the kernel.

#### Step 3: the full conditional of each $v_i$

The factors containing $v_i$ are those in the $i$-th term of the product:
$$
\begin{aligned}
p(v_i \mid \mu, \sigma^2, y) & \propto v_i^{-1/2}\, v_i^{-3/2}
\exp\Big\{-\frac{1}{v_i}\Big(\frac{(y_i-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2} + \frac12\Big)\Big\} \\
& = v_i^{-(1+1)} \exp\Big\{-\frac{(1 + r_i^2)/2}{v_i}\Big\}.
\end{aligned}
$$
This is the $\mathrm{IG}(a, b)$ kernel $v^{-(a+1)}e^{-b/v}$ with $a = 1$ and
$b = (1 + r_i^2)/2$:
$$
v_i \mid \mu, \sigma^2, y \sim \mathrm{IG}\Big(1,\ \frac{1 + r_i^2}{2}\Big), \qquad i = 1, \ldots, n,
$$
independently across $i$, since $v_i$ appears in no other factor. The scale
$(1 + r_i^2)/2$ grows with the standardized residual $r_i$, so an outlier
gets a large latent variance.

#### Step 4: the full conditional of $\mu$

The factors containing $\mu$ are the prior and the exponentials of the
likelihood. Writing $w_i = 1/(\sigma^2 v_i)$ for the precision of observation
$i$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
p(\mu \mid \sigma^2, v, y) & \propto \exp\Big\{-\frac{(\mu-\mu_0)^2}{2\tau^2} - \sum_i \frac{w_i (y_i-\mu)^2}{2}\Big\} \\
& \propto \exp\Big\{-\frac12\Big[\Big(\frac{1}{\tau^2} + \sum_i w_i\Big)\mu^2 - 2\Big(\frac{\mu_0}{\tau^2} + \sum_i w_i y_i\Big)\mu\Big]\Big\},
\end{aligned}
$$
after expanding the squares and dropping terms free of $\mu$. Completing the
square gives a normal distribution:
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mu \mid \sigma^2, v, y \sim N\big(m, s^2\big), \\
& \frac{1}{s^2} = \frac{1}{\tau^2} + \sum_{i=1}^n w_i, \qquad
m = s^2\Big(\frac{\mu_0}{\tau^2} + \sum_{i=1}^n w_i y_i\Big).
\end{aligned}
$$
This is a precision-weighted mean of the prior mean and the observations, as
in Example 2, except that each observation now has its own weight $w_i$. An
outlier, with a large $v_i$, has a small weight and barely moves $\mu$; this
is where the robustness of the Cauchy model comes from.

#### Step 5: the full conditional of $\sigma^2$

The factors containing $\sigma^2$ are its prior and the likelihood terms
$(\sigma^2)^{-1/2}$ and $\exp\{-(y_i-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2 v_i)\}$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
p(\sigma^2 \mid \mu, v, y) & \propto (\sigma^2)^{-(a_0+1)} e^{-b_0/\sigma^2} \cdot (\sigma^2)^{-n/2} \exp\Big\{-\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_i \frac{(y_i-\mu)^2}{2v_i}\Big\} \\
& = (\sigma^2)^{-(a_0 + \frac n2 + 1)} \exp\Big\{-\frac{b_0 + \sum_i (y_i-\mu)^2/(2v_i)}{\sigma^2}\Big\},
\end{aligned}
$$
again an inverse-gamma kernel:
$$
\sigma^2 \mid \mu, v, y \sim \mathrm{IG}\Big(a_0 + \frac n2,\ b_0 + \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{(y_i-\mu)^2}{2v_i}\Big).
$$

#### The sampler and a check against the exact posterior

One Gibbs iteration draws all $v_i$ (Step 3), then $\mu$ (Step 4), then
$\sigma^2$ (Step 5), each from its full conditional at the current values of
the others. We use $\mu_0 = 0$, $\tau = 10$ and $a_0 = b_0 = 1$, and 30
observations from $\text{Cauchy}(2, 1)$, which include several outliers
(the largest is above 35). Because the posterior of $(\mu, \sigma)$ is only
two-dimensional, it can also be computed exactly on a grid, which gives an
independent check of the sampler. On the $\sigma$ scale the prior density
is $p(\sigma^2)\cdot 2\sigma$, by the change of variable $\sigma^2 \to \sigma$.

```{r}
#| label: gibbs-cauchy
gibbs_cauchy <- function(iters, y, mu0 = 0, tau = 10, a0 = 1, b0 = 1, mu = 0, s2 = 1) {
    n <- length(y)
    out <- matrix(NA_real_, iters, 2, dimnames = list(NULL, c("mu", "sigma")))
    for (t in seq_len(iters)) {
        ### Step 3: v_i | mu, sigma^2 ~ IG(1, (1 + r_i^2) / 2), drawn as 1 / Gamma
        v <- 1 / rgamma(n, shape = 1, rate = (1 + (y - mu)^2 / s2) / 2)
        ### Step 4: mu | sigma^2, v ~ N(m, s^2), with observation weights w_i = 1 / (sigma^2 v_i)
        w <- 1 / (s2 * v)
        prec <- 1 / tau^2 + sum(w)
        mu <- rnorm(1, (mu0 / tau^2 + sum(w * y)) / prec, sqrt(1 / prec))
        ### Step 5: sigma^2 | mu, v ~ IG(a0 + n / 2, b0 + sum (y_i - mu)^2 / (2 v_i))
        s2 <- 1 / rgamma(1, shape = a0 + n / 2, rate = b0 + sum((y - mu)^2 / (2 * v)))
        out[t, ] <- c(mu, sqrt(s2))
    }
    out
}

### exact log posterior of (mu, sigma), up to a constant, for the grid check
log_post_cauchy <- function(mu, sigma, y, mu0 = 0, tau = 10, a0 = 1, b0 = 1) {
    sum(dcauchy(y, mu, sigma, log = TRUE)) + dnorm(mu, mu0, tau, log = TRUE) -
        (a0 + 1) * log(sigma^2) - b0 / sigma^2 + log(2 * sigma)
}

set.seed(7)
y_cauchy <- rcauchy(30, location = 2, scale = 1)
draws_cauchy <- gibbs_cauchy(20000, y_cauchy, mu = -5, s2 = 25)   # deliberately poor start
keep_c <- -(1:1000)

mu_grid <- seq(0, 4, length.out = 300); sg_grid <- seq(0.2, 3.5, length.out = 300)
lp <- outer(mu_grid, sg_grid, Vectorize(function(m, s) log_post_cauchy(m, s, y_cauchy)))
post <- exp(lp - max(lp)); post <- post / sum(post)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-gibbs-cauchy
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Demonstrates the data-augmentation Gibbs sampler for Cauchy data with unknown location and scale, checked against the exact posterior.
#|   Left: the first 15 iterations from a poor start (triangle), drawn as the staircase of
#|   mu- and sigma-updates, over the contours of the exact posterior computed on a grid.
#|   Middle and right: trace plots of mu and sigma for the first 500 iterations;
#|   the chain reaches the posterior within a few iterations."
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
contour(mu_grid, sg_grid, post, nlevels = 8, drawlabels = FALSE, col = "gray55",
        xlim = c(-5.5, 4), ylim = c(0, 5.5), xlab = expression(mu), ylab = expression(sigma),
        main = "first 15 iterations")
path <- rbind(c(-5, 5), draws_cauchy[1:15, ])
for (t in 1:15) {   # mu moves first (horizontal leg), then sigma (vertical leg)
    segments(path[t, 1], path[t, 2], path[t + 1, 1], path[t, 2], col = "darkorange", lwd = 1.5)
    segments(path[t + 1, 1], path[t, 2], path[t + 1, 1], path[t + 1, 2], col = "steelblue", lwd = 1.5)
}
points(-5, 5, pch = 17, cex = 1.4)
plot(draws_cauchy[1:500, "mu"], type = "l", col = "darkorange", xlab = "iteration",
     ylab = expression(mu), main = "trace of mu")
plot(draws_cauchy[1:500, "sigma"], type = "l", col = "steelblue", xlab = "iteration",
     ylab = expression(sigma), main = "trace of sigma")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-gibbs-cauchy
#| tbl-cap: "Checks the data-augmentation Gibbs sampler for the Cauchy model against the exact posterior computed on a grid.
#|   Posterior means and standard deviations of mu and sigma from 19,000 Gibbs draws (after a 1,000-iteration burn-in) and from the exact grid posterior. The sample median and the sample standard deviation are shown for contrast: the outliers inflate the standard deviation, while the Cauchy posterior is not affected by them."
grid_mean <- function(g, margin) sum(apply(post, margin, sum) * g)
grid_sd   <- function(g, margin) sqrt(sum(apply(post, margin, sum) * g^2) - grid_mean(g, margin)^2)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
    quantity = c("posterior mean of mu", "posterior sd of mu",
                 "posterior mean of sigma", "posterior sd of sigma"),
    gibbs = c(mean(draws_cauchy[keep_c, "mu"]), sd(draws_cauchy[keep_c, "mu"]),
              mean(draws_cauchy[keep_c, "sigma"]), sd(draws_cauchy[keep_c, "sigma"])),
    exact = c(grid_mean(mu_grid, 1), grid_sd(mu_grid, 1),
              grid_mean(sg_grid, 2), grid_sd(sg_grid, 2))
), digits = 3, col.names = c("quantity", "Gibbs", "exact (grid)"), align = c("l", "r", "r"))
```

The Gibbs estimates agree with the exact posterior to Monte Carlo error. For
comparison, the sample mean of these data is `r round(mean(y_cauchy), 2)` and
the sample standard deviation is `r round(sd(y_cauchy), 2)`, both dragged far
off by the outliers, while the posterior mean of $\mu$ stays near the centre of
the bulk of the data. []{#gibbs-cauchy-app}A [shinylive app](../../shinylive_apps/app_gibbs_cauchy.html) runs this sampler one conditional update at a time: it shows the $v$, $\mu$ and $\sigma$ updates as separate steps on the exact posterior, and the latent variances $v_i$ of the outliers.

## Metropolis–Hastings

### The algorithm

Gibbs sampling needs full conditionals that are both known and directly sample-able — a strong requirement outside conjugate models. **Metropolis–Hastings (MH)** needs only a target $\pi(\theta)$ computable up to a constant and *any* proposal distribution $\tilde T(\theta^* \mid \theta)$ we can sample from. Starting from $\theta^{(0)}$, repeat:

1. Draw a proposal $\theta^* \sim \tilde T(\cdot \mid \theta^{(t-1)})$.
2. Compute the acceptance ratio $r = \min\Big\{\dfrac{\pi(\theta^*)\,\tilde T(\theta^{(t-1)} \mid \theta^*)}{\pi(\theta^{(t-1)})\,\tilde T(\theta^* \mid \theta^{(t-1)})},\ 1\Big\}$.
3. With probability $r$ set $\theta^{(t)} = \theta^*$ (accept); otherwise set $\theta^{(t)} = \theta^{(t-1)}$ (reject **and repeat the current value**).

Only the ratio $\pi(\theta^*)/\pi(\theta^{(t-1)})$ is needed, so any normalizing constant of $\pi$ cancels — exactly as in rejection sampling, but here a rejected proposal still contributes a draw (the repeated current value) rather than being discarded, which is what lets MH work even when $\pi$ has no available envelope. One can show (by checking detailed balance directly, splitting into the "propose and accept" and "reject and stay" cases and using the $\min\{\cdot,\cdot\}$ identity $\min\{a,b\} = \min\{b,a\}$) that this $T$ leaves $\pi$ invariant regardless of what $\tilde T$ is, as long as its support is compatible with $\pi$'s.

### Random-walk Metropolis

If $\tilde T$ is symmetric, $\tilde T(\theta^* \mid \theta) = \tilde T(\theta \mid \theta^*)$ — e.g. $\theta^* \sim N(\theta^{(t-1)}, \varsigma^2)$ — the proposal terms cancel and $r = \min\{\pi(\theta^*)/\pi(\theta^{(t-1)}), 1\}$: uphill proposals are always accepted, downhill ones accepted in proportion to how much worse they are. $\varsigma$, the **step size**, is the only tuning parameter.

```{r}
#| label: met-gauss
met_gauss <- function(iters, log_f, stepsizes, ini_value, ...) {
    state <- ini_value; no_var <- length(state)
    logf <- log_f(ini_value, ...)
    if (!is.finite(logf)) stop("Initial value has zero probability")
    out <- matrix(NA_real_, iters, no_var); n_acc <- 0
    for (t in seq_len(iters)) {
        proposal <- rnorm(no_var, state, stepsizes)
        new_logf <- log_f(proposal, ...)
        if (log(runif(1)) < new_logf - logf) {
            state <- proposal; logf <- new_logf; n_acc <- n_acc + 1
        }
        out[t, ] <- state
    }
    attr(out, "accept_rate") <- n_acc / iters
    out
}
```

### Choosing the step size

The chain's draws are dependent, and what determines the precision of an ergodic average is not the acceptance rate itself but the resulting **autocorrelation**: for a stationary chain with lag-$k$ autocorrelation $\rho_k$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{Var}\Big(\tfrac1T\sum_{t=1}^T \theta^{(t)}\Big) & \approx \frac{\sigma^2}{T}\Big(1 + 2\sum_{k \ge 1} \rho_k\Big) \\
& = \frac{\sigma^2}{T_\text{eff}},
\end{aligned}
$$
so the tuning goal is small autocorrelation, not a high acceptance rate as such. A step too small is accepted almost every time but crawls (highly autocorrelated); a step too large is almost always rejected, so the chain barely moves either. Both extremes waste the same $T$ iterations on far fewer effective ones — the figure below (three step sizes on a $N(0,1)$ target) makes this visible directly in the trace and the ACF.

```{r}
#| label: fig-stepsize
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-cap: "Illustrates the trade-off in choosing the step size of a random-walk Metropolis-Hastings sampler, using trace plots and autocorrelation.
#|   Step size too small, about right, and too large: trace (top) and
#|   autocorrelation (bottom) for a random walk targeting N(0, 1)."
mh_std_normal <- function(sig, n = 2000) {
    th <- numeric(n); th[1] <- 0; acc <- 0
    for (t in 2:n) {
        p <- th[t - 1] + rnorm(1, 0, sig)
        if (runif(1) < dnorm(p) / dnorm(th[t - 1])) { th[t] <- p; acc <- acc + 1 } else th[t] <- th[t - 1]
    }
    list(th = th, acc = acc / (n - 1))
}
res <- lapply(c(0.1, 2.4, 40), mh_std_normal)
labs <- c("too small", "about right", "too large")
par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (k in 1:3) plot(res[[k]]$th[1:500], type = "l", col = "steelblue", xlab = "t", ylab = expression(theta^(t)),
                     ylim = c(-3.5, 3.5), main = sprintf("%s: accept %.2f", labs[k], res[[k]]$acc))
for (k in 1:3) acf(res[[k]]$th, lag.max = 50, main = "ACF")
```

For random-walk Metropolis on a smooth target, theory recommends an acceptance rate near $0.234$ in high dimension (up to about $0.44$ in one dimension) as the rate that minimizes autocorrelation for a given computational budget — a useful rule of thumb, not a target to hit exactly.

### Metropolis-within-Gibbs

The two ideas combine directly. If $\theta = (\theta_1, \theta_2)$ and $\pi(\theta_1 \mid \theta_2)$ has no convenient sampler while $\pi(\theta_2 \mid \theta_1)$ does, replace only the first Gibbs step by a Metropolis–Hastings update that targets $\pi(\theta_1 \mid \theta_2)$ (evaluated at the *current* $\theta_2$) and leave the second step as an exact conditional draw. Each block transition leaves $\pi$ invariant on its own — the Gibbs argument applies verbatim to any $\pi(\theta_j \mid \theta_{-j})$-invariant transition, not only an exact conditional draw — so the composite sweep leaves the full joint $\pi$ invariant. This "Gibbs where conjugate, Metropolis elsewhere" pattern, iterated one parameter or block at a time, is how most general-purpose Bayesian software before Hamiltonian methods actually worked.

### Example 5: A Normal Truncated to Its Tail

**The problem.** Draw from $N(0, 2^2)$ truncated to $[4, 5]$, a sliver of the far right tail,
$$
\pi(\theta) \propto \varphi\Big(\frac{\theta}{2}\Big)\, I(4 \le \theta \le 5).
$$
Sampling from $N(0, 2^2)$ and keeping the draws that land in $[4, 5]$ is exact but wasteful: only a fraction $\Phi(2.5) - \Phi(2) \approx `r sprintf("%.3f", pnorm(2.5) - pnorm(2))`$ of the draws is kept, about one in `r round(1 / (pnorm(2.5) - pnorm(2)))`, and a target further in the tail would be worse still.

**Random-walk Metropolis.** The indicator needs no special handling: a proposal landing outside $[4, 5]$ has $\pi(\theta^*) = 0$, hence $r = 0$, and is automatically rejected, while inside the interval the acceptance probability is the ratio of normal densities. Starting inside the interval, the chain never leaves it, and every iteration produces a draw. @fig-tnorm-mh runs `met_gauss` with three step sizes and reports the acceptance rate and the effective sample size $T_\text{eff}$ of each chain.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tnorm-mh
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-cap: "Demonstrates random-walk Metropolis-Hastings on a normal distribution truncated to its tail, where sampling the untruncated normal and keeping the draws in range is wasteful.
#|   Random-walk MH targeting N(0, 2^2) truncated to [4, 5], for three step sizes, with the acceptance
#|   rate and effective sample size (ESS) of each chain of 5,000 iterations."
log_tnorm <- function(x, mu, sigma, lb, ub) {
    if (x > lb && x < ub) dnorm(x, mu, sigma, log = TRUE) else -Inf
}
set.seed(6); steps <- c(0.1, 1, 2)
mcs <- lapply(steps, function(st) met_gauss(5000, log_tnorm, stepsizes = st, ini_value = 4.5,
                                            mu = 0, sigma = 2, lb = 4, ub = 5))
ess_fn <- function(th) {                 # effective sample size T / (1 + 2 sum rho_k), summed to the first rho_k < 0
    rho <- acf(th, lag.max = 200, plot = FALSE)$acf[-1]
    k <- which(rho < 0)[1]; if (is.na(k)) k <- length(rho) + 1
    length(th) / (1 + 2 * sum(rho[seq_len(k - 1)]))
}
ess <- sapply(mcs, ess_fn)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (k in 1:3) plot(mcs[[k]], type = "l", col = "steelblue", xlab = "iteration", ylab = expression(theta),
    main = sprintf("step = %.1f, accept = %.2f, ESS = %.0f", steps[k], attr(mcs[[k]], "accept_rate"), ess[k]))
```

The three chains differ in how efficiently they explore $[4, 5]$, as measured by the effective sample size; as in @fig-stepsize, the smallest step is accepted most often but moves least. The chain with the largest ESS, step $`r steps[which.max(ess)]`$, reproduces the exact truncated density (@fig-tnorm-density), including its decline across the interval: $\varphi$ is decreasing there, so states near $4$ are visited about $`r sprintf("%.1f", dnorm(4, 0, 2) / dnorm(5, 0, 2))`$ times as often as states near $5$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tnorm-density
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-cap: "Checks the random-walk Metropolis-Hastings sampler for the truncated normal against the exact density.
#|   Histogram of the 5,000 states of the chain with the largest effective sample size, with the exact
#|   N(0, 2^2) density truncated to [4, 5] (dashed)."
best <- which.max(ess); th_best <- mcs[[best]][, 1]
par(mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
hist(th_best, breaks = 40, freq = FALSE, col = "gray85", border = "white", xlim = c(3.9, 5.1),
     xlab = expression(theta), ylab = "density",
     main = sprintf("step = %.1f (accept %.2f)", steps[best], attr(mcs[[best]], "accept_rate")))
curve(dnorm(x, 0, 2) / (pnorm(5, 0, 2) - pnorm(4, 0, 2)), 4, 5, add = TRUE, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("topright", bty = "n", lwd = c(NA, 2), lty = c(NA, 2), pch = c(15, NA), pt.cex = 2,
       col = c("gray85", "firebrick"), legend = c("histogram of the draws", "exact truncated normal density"))
```

### Example 6: Normal Data with Unknown Mean and Variance, Revisited

This is the model, prior and data of Example 2,
$$
x_1, \ldots, x_n \mid \mu, \sigma^2 \overset{iid}{\sim} N(\mu, \sigma^2), \qquad \mu \sim N(\mu_0, \sigma_0^2), \qquad \sigma^2 \sim \mathrm{IG}(a_0, \lambda_0),
$$
now sampled by random-walk Metropolis–Hastings.

**The model on the log scale.** $\sigma^2 > 0$ makes a symmetric normal random walk directly on $\sigma^2$ wasteful (many proposals land below zero and are rejected), so reparametrize
$$
w = \log \sigma^2 \in \mathbb R, \qquad \sigma^2 = e^w.
$$
By the change-of-variables formula, if $X \sim f_X$ and $Y = t(X)$, then $f_Y(y) = f_X\big(t^{-1}(y)\big)\,\big|\tfrac{d t^{-1}(y)}{dy}\big|$. Here $t^{-1}(w) = e^w$, so the Jacobian is $e^w$, and
$$
P(\mu, w \mid x) \ \propto\
\underbrace{e^{-\frac{(\mu-\mu_0)^2}{2\sigma_0^2}}}_{p(\mu)} \cdot
\underbrace{(e^w)^{-(a_0+1)} e^{-\lambda_0 e^{-w}}}_{p_{\sigma^2}(e^w)} \cdot
\underbrace{(e^w)^{-n/2} e^{-\sum_i (x_i-\mu)^2 e^{-w}/2}}_{\text{likelihood}} \cdot
\underbrace{e^w}_{\text{Jacobian}}.
$$
Collecting the powers of $e^w$, $-(a_0+1) - \tfrac n2 + 1 = -(a_0 + \tfrac n2)$, so
$$
\log P(\mu, w \mid x) = -\frac{(\mu-\mu_0)^2}{2\sigma_0^2} - \Big(a_0 + \frac n2\Big) w - \Big(\lambda_0 + \frac12 \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \mu)^2\Big) e^{-w} + \text{const}.
$$
Omitting the Jacobian $e^w$ would target the wrong distribution.

**The sampler.** A random-walk proposal on $(\mu, w)$ jointly, with `met_gauss` from above; the log posterior in the code is the formula above, term by term:

```{r}
#| label: mh-normal
log_post_mu_w <- function(mu, w)                    # prior constants mu0, s02, a0, lam0 from Example 2
    -(mu - mu0)^2 / (2 * s02) - (a0 + length(x) / 2) * w - (lam0 + sum((x - mu)^2) / 2) * exp(-w)
mh_norm <- function(iters, stepsizes) {
    mc <- met_gauss(iters, function(th) log_post_mu_w(th[1], th[2]), stepsizes, ini_value = c(0, 0))
    list(mu = mc[, 1], sd = exp(mc[, 2] / 2), accept_rate = attr(mc, "accept_rate"))   # sigma = e^{w/2}
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-mh-stepsize-search
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-cap: "Illustrates how to tune the step size in practice, by comparing short preliminary runs at several scales.
#|   Preliminary MH runs at four step-size scales, targeting mu (top:
#|   trace, bottom: ACF after discarding 500 iterations)."
set.seed(5)
scales <- c(20, 10, 4, 2)
fits <- lapply(scales, function(s) mh_norm(10000, c(s, s) / sqrt(length(x))))
par(mfcol = c(2, 4), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (k in seq_along(fits)) {
    plot(fits[[k]]$mu[1:1000], type = "l", col = "steelblue", xlab = "t", ylab = expression(mu),
         main = sprintf("scale %g, accept %.2f", scales[k], fits[[k]]$accept_rate))
    acf(fits[[k]]$mu[-(1:500)], main = "ACF")
}
```

Scale $4$ gives the least autocorrelated trace among the four, consistent with an acceptance rate closer to the $0.2$–$0.4$ range than the very low or very high rates at the extremes. The posterior densities estimated from that chain already match those of the Gibbs sampler (@fig-mh-best-density).

```{r}
#| label: fig-mh-best-density
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-cap: "Compares the posterior densities from the best-tuned Metropolis-Hastings chain with those from the Gibbs sampler.
#|   Kernel densities of mu and sigma from the scale-4 chain of the preliminary runs (10,000 iterations,
#|   first 500 discarded; solid) and from the Gibbs sampler of Example 2 (dashed)."
best5 <- fits[[3]]; keep5 <- -(1:500)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(density(best5$mu[keep5]), col = "steelblue", lwd = 2, xlab = expression(mu), main = "posterior density of mu")
lines(density(mu_g), col = "gray30", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("topright", bty = "n", lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 2), col = c("steelblue", "gray30"), legend = c("MH, scale 4", "Gibbs"))
plot(density(best5$sd[keep5]), col = "firebrick", lwd = 2, xlab = expression(sigma), main = "posterior density of sigma")
lines(density(sd_g), col = "gray30", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("topright", bty = "n", lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 2), col = c("firebrick", "gray30"), legend = c("MH, scale 4", "Gibbs"))
```

Running a long chain at that scale and comparing to the Gibbs sampler on the same data:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mh-vs-gibbs
#| tbl-cap: "Checks the Metropolis-Hastings sampler against Gibbs sampling on the same problem.
#|   Posterior mean and sd from Metropolis-Hastings versus Gibbs sampling, same data and priors: the two exact samplers of the same posterior agree up to Monte Carlo error."
mh_long <- mh_norm(50000, c(4, 4) / sqrt(length(x)))
keep_mh <- -(1:1000)
coherence <- data.frame(
    method = c("Metropolis-Hastings", "Gibbs"),
    mean_mu = c(mean(mh_long$mu[keep_mh]), mean(mu_g)),
    sd_mu   = c(sd(mh_long$mu[keep_mh]), sd(mu_g)),
    mean_sigma = c(mean(mh_long$sd[keep_mh]), mean(sd_g)),
    sd_sigma   = c(sd(mh_long$sd[keep_mh]), sd(sd_g))
)
knitr::kable(coherence, digits = 3, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

## Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and Stan

### Why random walks struggle

A random-walk proposal has no sense of direction: reaching a point one posterior standard deviation away takes $O(d)$ steps in $d$ dimensions, and far more along a narrow, correlated ridge, since most proposed directions immediately step off the ridge and get rejected. Gibbs suffers the same way when parameters are strongly correlated, since each step moves along only one coordinate axis. **Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC)** uses the *gradient* $\nabla \log \pi(\theta)$ to propose points far away with high probability of acceptance.

Introduce an auxiliary **momentum** variable $p \in \mathbb R^d$ and the joint density $\pi(\theta, p) \propto \exp\{-H(\theta,p)\}$ with
$$
H(\theta, p) = \underbrace{-\log \pi(\theta)}_{\text{potential } U(\theta)} + \underbrace{\tfrac12 p^\top M^{-1} p}_{\text{kinetic } K(p)},
$$
so that the $\theta$-marginal is exactly the target and $p \sim N_d(0, M)$ independently. Physically: a particle at position $\theta$ with momentum $p$ rolling frictionlessly on the potential surface $U(\theta)$. Hamilton's equations move $(\theta,p)$ so as to *conserve* $H$ exactly and are volume-preserving and reversible; discretizing them with the **leapfrog** integrator (step size $\epsilon$, $L$ steps),
$$
\begin{aligned}
p & \leftarrow p + \tfrac\epsilon2 \nabla\log\pi(\theta), \qquad \theta \leftarrow \theta + \epsilon M^{-1}p, \\
p & \leftarrow p + \tfrac\epsilon2\nabla\log\pi(\theta),
\end{aligned}
$$
keeps volume-preservation and reversibility exactly (negating $p$ and re-running gives back the start) while introducing only an $O(\epsilon^2)$ error in $H$, which a Metropolis accept/reject step then corrects exactly.

### The algorithm

Starting from $\theta^{(0)}$, repeat: draw a fresh $p \sim N_d(0,M)$; run $L$ leapfrog steps from $(\theta^{(t-1)}, p)$ to reach $(\theta^*, p^*)$; accept $\theta^{(t)} = \theta^*$ with probability $\min\{\exp[H(\theta^{(t-1)},p) - H(\theta^*,p^*)], 1\}$, else repeat $\theta^{(t-1)}$. Drawing $p$ is a Gibbs step from its own conditional (it doesn't depend on $\theta$), and the leapfrog-plus-accept step is a Metropolis update with a deterministic, reversible proposal — so each half leaves $\pi(\theta,p)$ invariant, and because $H$ is nearly conserved, acceptance stays high (typically $0.65$–$0.8$) even though $\theta^*$ may be far from $\theta^{(t-1)}$.

```{r}
#| label: hmc-fn
hmc <- function(log_pi, grad_log_pi, theta, eps, L, iters, M = diag(length(theta))) {
    d <- length(theta); Minv <- solve(M); R <- chol(M)
    out <- matrix(NA_real_, iters, d); n_acc <- 0
    for (t in seq_len(iters)) {
        p0 <- as.vector(t(R) %*% rnorm(d))
        th <- theta; p <- p0 + eps / 2 * grad_log_pi(th)
        for (l in seq_len(L)) {
            th <- th + eps * as.vector(Minv %*% p)
            if (l < L) p <- p + eps * grad_log_pi(th)
        }
        p <- p + eps / 2 * grad_log_pi(th)
        H0 <- -log_pi(theta) + 0.5 * sum(p0 * (Minv %*% p0))
        H1 <- -log_pi(th)    + 0.5 * sum(p  * (Minv %*% p))
        if (log(runif(1)) < H0 - H1) { theta <- th; n_acc <- n_acc + 1 }
        out[t, ] <- theta
    }
    attr(out, "accept_rate") <- n_acc / iters
    out
}
```

### Example 7: Bivariate Normal with Correlation 0.98

A strongly correlated bivariate normal is the simplest target on which a random walk struggles. Both samplers below get the same budget of 2,000 iterations and start from the same point.

```{r}
#| label: fig-hmc-vs-rw
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-cap: "Compares Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with random-walk Metropolis on a highly correlated target, where the random walk struggles.
#|   Target: bivariate normal with correlation 0.98. Left/middle: first
#|   100 draws over the posterior contours for random-walk Metropolis and HMC,
#|   same iteration budget. Right: autocorrelation of the first coordinate --
#|   HMC crosses the ridge in one trajectory and its draws decorrelate almost
#|   immediately."
set.seed(4)
Sigma <- matrix(c(1, 0.98, 0.98, 1), 2); Sinv <- solve(Sigma)
log_pi_corr  <- function(z) -0.5 * sum(z * (Sinv %*% z))
grad_pi_corr <- function(z) -as.vector(Sinv %*% z)

rw <- matrix(NA_real_, 2000, 2); cur <- c(-2, -2); lp <- log_pi_corr(cur); acc <- 0
for (t in 1:2000) {
    pr <- cur + 0.3 * rnorm(2); lpp <- log_pi_corr(pr)
    if (log(runif(1)) < lpp - lp) { cur <- pr; lp <- lpp; acc <- acc + 1 }
    rw[t, ] <- cur
}
draws_hmc <- hmc(log_pi_corr, grad_pi_corr, theta = c(-2, -2), eps = 0.05, L = 30, iters = 2000)

g <- seq(-3.5, 3.5, length.out = 80)
Z <- outer(g, g, Vectorize(function(a, b) exp(-0.5 * c(a, b) %*% Sinv %*% c(a, b))))
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (nm in c("random walk", "HMC")) {
    d <- if (nm == "random walk") rw else draws_hmc
    ar <- if (nm == "random walk") acc / 2000 else attr(draws_hmc, "accept_rate")
    contour(g, g, Z, nlevels = 6, drawlabels = FALSE, col = "gray60",
            xlab = expression(theta[1]), ylab = expression(theta[2]),
            main = sprintf("%s: accept %.2f", nm, ar))
    lines(d[1:100, ], col = if (nm == "random walk") "firebrick" else "steelblue", lwd = 1.5)
    points(d[1:100, ], pch = 19, cex = 0.5, col = if (nm == "random walk") "firebrick" else "steelblue")
}
a1 <- acf(rw[, 1], lag.max = 60, plot = FALSE)$acf
a2 <- acf(draws_hmc[, 1], lag.max = 60, plot = FALSE)$acf
plot(0:60, a1, type = "h", lwd = 2, col = "firebrick", xlab = "lag", ylab = "ACF", ylim = c(-0.2, 1), main = "autocorrelation")
lines((0:60) + 0.3, a2, type = "h", lwd = 2, col = "steelblue")
legend("topright", bty = "n", lwd = 2, col = c("firebrick", "steelblue"), legend = c("random walk", "HMC"))
```

Chi Feng's [MCMC simulators](https://chi-feng.github.io/mcmc-demo/app.html) let you tune the step size and number of leapfrog steps of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, and compare it with other samplers, to see how they affect its exploration of a correlated target.


### Stan: automating HMC

Every sampler above needed something derived by hand: Gibbs needed full conditionals worked out algebraically; Metropolis–Hastings needed only a target density but still needed step sizes tuned by trial and error; HMC needed an analytic gradient and needed $\epsilon$ and $L$ tuned by hand. **Stan** is a probabilistic programming language that automates all of this: given a model written declaratively (data, parameters, and a log-density), it computes gradients by automatic differentiation and runs an adaptive variant of HMC — the **No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS)**, which picks a good $L$ on the fly by extending the leapfrog trajectory until it starts to double back — with step size tuned during a warm-up phase. The user never derives a conditional or a gradient.

### Where Stan earns its keep

The normal-mean/variance model of Examples 2 and 6 is simple enough that Gibbs sampling is not just possible but easy, so Stan's advantage is not visible yet. Its real value shows up on models where hand-deriving conditionals or gradients would be a serious undertaking: hierarchical models with many levels of latent structure, time-series models with an unobserved latent state at every time point, or anything with a non-conjugate likelihood/prior combination. Example 9 gives a small taste of this: the Cauchy model needed a scale-mixture trick and three derivations for Gibbs sampling, but only its model statement in Stan.

### Example 8: Normal Data with Unknown Mean and Variance, in Stan

To confirm Stan lands on the same posterior as the Gibbs and MH samplers of Examples 2 and 6, fit the identical normal-mean/variance model with the identical priors and data:

```{r}
#| label: stan-model-normal
stan_normal_code <- "
data {
  int<lower=0> n;
  vector[n] x;
  real mu0;
  real<lower=0> s02;
  real<lower=0> a0;
  real<lower=0> lam0;
}
parameters {
  real mu;
  real<lower=0> sigma2;
}
model {
  mu ~ normal(mu0, sqrt(s02));
  sigma2 ~ inv_gamma(a0, lam0);
  x ~ normal(mu, sqrt(sigma2));
}
"
```

```{r}
#| label: stan-fit-normal
#| cache: true
#| message: false
fit_stan <- stan(
    model_code = stan_normal_code,
    data = list(n = length(x), x = x, mu0 = mu0, s02 = s02, a0 = a0, lam0 = lam0),
    chains = 4, iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, seed = 5, refresh = 0
)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-stan-vs-hand
#| tbl-cap: "Validates Stan's sampler against the samplers written by hand earlier in the chapter.
#|   Posterior mean and sd: hand-written Gibbs and Metropolis-Hastings versus Stan's NUTS sampler, same data, priors, and model. All three samplers target the identical posterior and agree up to Monte Carlo error."
stan_summary <- summary(fit_stan, pars = c("mu", "sigma2"))$summary
stan_sigma_draws <- sqrt(as.matrix(fit_stan, pars = "sigma2")[, 1])
three_way <- data.frame(
    method = c("Gibbs", "Metropolis-Hastings", "Stan (NUTS)"),
    mean_mu = c(mean(mu_g), mean(mh_long$mu[keep_mh]), stan_summary["mu", "mean"]),
    sd_mu   = c(sd(mu_g), sd(mh_long$mu[keep_mh]), stan_summary["mu", "sd"]),
    mean_sigma = c(mean(sd_g), mean(mh_long$sd[keep_mh]), mean(stan_sigma_draws)),
    sd_sigma   = c(sd(sd_g), sd(mh_long$sd[keep_mh]), sd(stan_sigma_draws))
)
knitr::kable(three_way, digits = 3, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

The three completely independent implementations — hand-derived conditionals, a hand-tuned random walk, and Stan's automatic NUTS — agree to within Monte Carlo noise, which is exactly the coherence check this book has used throughout: independent methods with no shared code path landing on the same answer is evidence that none of them is wrong.

### Example 9: Cauchy Data with Unknown Location and Scale, in Stan

Example 4 needed a page of algebra: a scale-mixture representation, an
augmented posterior, and three full conditionals. In Stan none of that is
needed. The model is written exactly as stated in Example 4, with the Cauchy
likelihood used directly and no latent variances, and NUTS samples the
two-dimensional posterior of $(\mu, \sigma^2)$ using gradients from
automatic differentiation. The data and priors are those of Example 4:
$\mu \sim N(0, 10^2)$, $\sigma^2 \sim \mathrm{IG}(1, 1)$ and the same 30
observations.

```{r}
#| label: stan-model-cauchy
stan_cauchy_code <- "
data {
  int<lower=0> n;
  vector[n] y;
  real mu0;
  real<lower=0> tau;
  real<lower=0> a0;
  real<lower=0> b0;
}
parameters {
  real mu;
  real<lower=0> sigma2;
}
transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0> sigma = sqrt(sigma2);
}
model {
  mu ~ normal(mu0, tau);
  sigma2 ~ inv_gamma(a0, b0);
  y ~ cauchy(mu, sigma);
}
"
```

```{r}
#| label: stan-fit-cauchy
#| cache: true
#| message: false
fit_cauchy_stan <- stan(
    model_code = stan_cauchy_code,
    data = list(n = length(y_cauchy), y = y_cauchy, mu0 = 0, tau = 10, a0 = 1, b0 = 1),
    chains = 4, iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, seed = 8, refresh = 0
)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-stan-cauchy
#| tbl-cap: "Checks Stan's NUTS sampler for the Cauchy model against the data-augmentation Gibbs sampler of Example 4 and the exact grid posterior.
#|   Posterior means and standard deviations of mu and sigma, same data and priors. Stan samples the Cauchy likelihood directly, without latent variables; all three agree up to Monte Carlo error."
st_c <- as.matrix(fit_cauchy_stan, pars = c("mu", "sigma"))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
    quantity = c("posterior mean of mu", "posterior sd of mu",
                 "posterior mean of sigma", "posterior sd of sigma"),
    gibbs = c(mean(draws_cauchy[keep_c, "mu"]), sd(draws_cauchy[keep_c, "mu"]),
              mean(draws_cauchy[keep_c, "sigma"]), sd(draws_cauchy[keep_c, "sigma"])),
    stan = c(mean(st_c[, "mu"]), sd(st_c[, "mu"]), mean(st_c[, "sigma"]), sd(st_c[, "sigma"])),
    exact = c(grid_mean(mu_grid, 1), grid_sd(mu_grid, 1),
              grid_mean(sg_grid, 2), grid_sd(sg_grid, 2))
), digits = 3, col.names = c("quantity", "Gibbs (Example 4)", "Stan (NUTS)", "exact (grid)"),
   align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"))
```

```{r}
#| label: stan-cauchy-diagnostics
summary(fit_cauchy_stan, pars = c("mu", "sigma"))$summary[, c("mean", "sd", "n_eff", "Rhat")]
```

The three answers agree, and $\hat R \approx 1$ with effective sample sizes
in the thousands shows that the four chains have mixed. The comparison shows
the trade-off between the two approaches. The Gibbs sampler of Example 4
needs no tuning and each iteration is cheap, but it needed the scale-mixture
trick and three derivations. Stan needed only the model statement, and it
would work unchanged with a different prior or a Student-$t$ likelihood with
any degrees of freedom, where the Gibbs derivation would have to be redone.

## A Final Practical Example: Sparse Logistic Regression

The examples so far were chosen to show how each sampler works, on models small enough to check against an exact answer. This section puts the pieces together on a problem where Bayesian computation earns its place in practice: a logistic regression with as many unknowns as there are cases, where maximum likelihood breaks down, the prior decides the quality of the answer, and Stan makes the fit routine. The posterior is compared with two standard non-Bayesian fits, `glm` and the LASSO, on new test data.

### The problem

Binary responses $y_1, \ldots, y_n$ depend on $p$ candidate
predictors through the logistic regression model
$$
y_i \mid \alpha, \beta \sim \text{Bernoulli}\big(\text{logit}^{-1}(\alpha + x_i^\top \beta)\big),
\qquad \text{logit}^{-1}(\eta) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\eta}}.
$$
Here there are $p = 50$ predictors for only $n = 100$ cases. The predictors
are standard normal and only two carry signal: the true values are
$\alpha = 0$, $\beta_1 = 1$, $\beta_2 = -1$ and $\beta_3 = \cdots = \beta_{50} = 0$.

### Why maximum likelihood fails

With 51 unknowns and only 100 cases, it is
very likely, and true for these data, that some linear combination
$\alpha + x_i^\top\beta$ is positive for every case with $y_i = 1$ and negative
for every case with $y_i = 0$: the data are perfectly **separable**.
Multiplying such a $\beta$ by a larger and larger constant pushes every fitted
probability towards its observed $0$ or $1$, so the likelihood keeps
increasing and the MLE does not exist. `glm` stops after a fixed number of
iterations with very large coefficients (here up to about $60$ in absolute
value) and warns that the algorithm did not converge and that fitted
probabilities are numerically $0$ or $1$.

### A sparse prior: the horseshoe

A Bayesian fit always has a proper posterior, but the prior
now matters a great deal. A vague prior such as $\beta_j \sim N(0, 2.5^2)$
lets all 48 null coefficients wander, and their sum swamps the signal. We
want a prior that says *most coefficients are near 0, but a few may be
large*. The **horseshoe prior** does this with two levels of scale:
$$
\beta_j = \tau\,\lambda_j\, z_j, \qquad z_j \sim N(0, 1), \qquad
\lambda_j \sim \text{Cauchy}^+(0, 1), \qquad \tau \sim \text{Cauchy}^+(0, 0.1),
$$
where $\text{Cauchy}^+$ is the Cauchy distribution restricted to positive
values. The **global** scale $\tau$ is small, so it shrinks every coefficient
strongly towards $0$. The **local** scale $\lambda_j$ has a heavy tail, so a
coefficient that the data support can take a large $\lambda_j$ and escape the
shrinkage. The intercept gets $\alpha \sim N(0, 5^2)$. Writing $\beta_j$ as a
product with a standard normal $z_j$ is the non-centred form used for Stan,
and a smaller step size (`adapt_delta = 0.995`) helps NUTS handle the very
different scales of $\tau$ and the $\lambda_j$, which otherwise cause many
divergent transitions. If a handful remain, Stan reports them as a warning;
with only a few out of 8,000 draws, $\hat R$ near 1 and large effective sample
sizes, they would not noticeably affect the summaries.

### Fitting in Stan

The horseshoe model in Stan, and the same model with the vague normal prior for comparison:

```{r}
#| label: stan-model-logit
stan_logit_hs_code <- "
data {
  int<lower=0> n;
  int<lower=1> p;
  matrix[n, p] X;
  array[n] int<lower=0, upper=1> y;
}
parameters {
  real alpha;
  real<lower=0> tau;             // global scale
  vector<lower=0>[p] lambda;     // local scales
  vector[p] z;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[p] beta = tau * lambda .* z;
}
model {
  alpha ~ normal(0, 5);
  tau ~ cauchy(0, 0.1);
  lambda ~ cauchy(0, 1);
  z ~ std_normal();
  y ~ bernoulli_logit(alpha + X * beta);
}
"
### the same model with a vague normal prior on every coefficient, for comparison
stan_logit_normal_code <- "
data {
  int<lower=0> n;
  int<lower=1> p;
  matrix[n, p] X;
  array[n] int<lower=0, upper=1> y;
}
parameters {
  real alpha;
  vector[p] beta;
}
model {
  alpha ~ normal(0, 5);
  beta ~ normal(0, 2.5);
  y ~ bernoulli_logit(alpha + X * beta);
}
"
```

```{r}
#| label: stan-fit-logit
#| cache: true
#| message: false
set.seed(2024)
n_lr <- 100; p_lr <- 50
X_lr <- matrix(rnorm(n_lr * p_lr), n_lr, p_lr)
beta_true <- c(1, -1, rep(0, p_lr - 2))
y_lr <- rbinom(n_lr, 1, plogis(drop(X_lr %*% beta_true)))
data_lr <- list(n = n_lr, p = p_lr, X = X_lr, y = y_lr)
fit_logit <- stan(model_code = stan_logit_hs_code, data = data_lr,
                  chains = 4, iter = 3000, warmup = 1000, seed = 9, refresh = 0,
                  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.995))
fit_logit_normal <- stan(model_code = stan_logit_normal_code, data = data_lr,
                         chains = 4, iter = 2000, warmup = 1000, seed = 9, refresh = 0)
```

### The horseshoe posterior

@tbl-stan-logit summarizes the horseshoe posterior of the first ten
coefficients: the two signals and eight of the 48 nulls.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-stan-logit
#| tbl-cap: "Summarizes the posterior distribution of the first ten coefficients of a logistic regression with 50 predictors and 100 cases, under the horseshoe prior. Only the first two coefficients carry signal.
#|   Posterior mean, standard deviation and 95% credible interval from 8,000 NUTS draws, next to the true value. Rhat near 1 and large effective sample sizes show that the chains have mixed."
sm_logit <- summary(fit_logit, pars = sprintf("beta[%d]", 1:10))$summary
knitr::kable(data.frame(
    coefficient = sprintf("beta[%d]", 1:10),
    true = beta_true[1:10],
    mean = sm_logit[, "mean"], sd = sm_logit[, "sd"],
    q025 = sm_logit[, "2.5%"], q975 = sm_logit[, "97.5%"],
    n_eff = round(sm_logit[, "n_eff"]), Rhat = sm_logit[, "Rhat"],
    row.names = NULL),
    digits = c(0, 0, 3, 3, 3, 3, 0, 3),
    col.names = c("coefficient", "true", "mean", "sd", "2.5%", "97.5%", "n_eff", "Rhat"),
    align = c("l", rep("r", 7)))
```

The null coefficients are shrunk tightly around $0$, with posterior standard
deviations near $0.1$. The two signals escape the shrinkage: their posterior
means are close to the true values $1$ and $-1$, and both 95% intervals
exclude $0$. @fig-stan-logit shows the posterior draws of the two signals and
two of the nulls.

```{r}
#| label: fig-stan-logit
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Shows the posterior distributions of two signal and two null coefficients in a logistic regression with 50 predictors and 100 cases, under the horseshoe prior.
#|   Histograms of 8,000 NUTS draws of beta_1 and beta_2 (signals, top) and beta_3 and beta_4
#|   (nulls, bottom). The red line marks the true value and the dashed line marks 0. The null
#|   posteriors are concentrated at 0; the signal posteriors are centred near the true values,
#|   with only a small spike at 0 for beta_1."
draws_beta <- as.matrix(fit_logit, pars = "beta")
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 1))
for (j in 1:4) {
    hist(draws_beta[, j], breaks = 60, freq = FALSE, col = "gray80", border = "white",
```
